headline: Sort meetings and inspect neighboring boundaries
statement: Given meeting intervals [start,end), return whether one person can attend every meeting. A meeting ending at time t does not conflict with one beginning at t. The empty schedule is attendable.
prerequisites: Basic Python lists, loops, and functions
intuition: Sort the meetings by starting time. Then compare each meeting with the one before it. If the next meeting starts before the previous one ends, one person cannot attend both. If every neighboring pair fits, the whole schedule fits.
approach: Sort a copy of intervals by start time.
For each interval after the first, compare its start to the previous end.
Return false for a strict start<previous_end overlap.
Return true after every neighbor passes.
correctness: If a neighboring pair overlaps, attendance is impossible. Conversely, if every neighbor is nonoverlapping, each interval ends no later than the next begins. Chaining these inequalities shows any earlier interval ends before any later interval begins, so there are no conflicts anywhere.
bruteForce: Compare every pair of meetings in O(n^2) time. Sorting exposes enough structure to check only neighbors.

complexity.explanation: The sorted copy and Python sorting workspace use linear storage; the neighbor scan is linear.

pitfalls: Touching endpoints are allowed: use < rather than <= for overlap.
An empty list and a single meeting both return true.
